newsitem.title: USA: World Bank rejects Bangladesh project probe calls.
newsitem.headline: World Bank rejects Bangladesh project probe calls.

text.p: The World Bank said on Wednesday it was unnecessary to investigate complaints against the $600 million Jamuna Bridge project in Bangladesh and a separate loan to restructure the jute sector there.

Construction of a bridge over the Jamuna River, the country's biggest infrastructure project, has drawn protests from leaders of some 70,000 people who live on 75 islands, known as chars, in the project area.
The shifting river, causing flooding and erosion, is a major complicating factor for the project, the bank said.

An Inspection Panel found that the 1993 resettlement plan did not specifically cover the char people, the bank said. But a September 1996 erosion and flood policy document "could constitute an adequate and enforceable basis...to meet the char dwellers' concerns," the bank said.
It said its board accepted the panel recommendations that there was no need to investigate the project at this time, and called for a progress report in April 1998.
The bank also accepted the panel's recommendations that it was unnecessary to investigate government restructuring of the jute sector, which is backed by a World Bank loan.
But the bank said the project would not be extended beyond its June 1997 closing date, unless an upcoming mission sees substantial progress in privatising jute mills.
An extension would only be granted against a tight schedule for completing the programme, the bank said.
Private sector jute mill operators have said the project, designed to promote a healthy private sector, has instead resulted in financial damage and closure of some private jute mills.

The World Bank approved a credit of $247 million in 1994 to help the Bangladesh government restructure the jute sector. The bank, the Asian Development Bank and Japan's Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund are providing $200 million each for the Jamuna Bridge project.
